description: We are a passionate team of students from the Department of Digital Systems at the University of Thessaly. Driven by curiosity and a shared love for technology, we combine our skills in software development, data analysis, and digital innovation to solve real-world space and Earth challenges. Our goal is to transform complex data into impactful, user-friendly digital solutions that can make a difference.
summary:
Degrees of Sound turns NASA's global temperature maps into music, so anyone can explore climate change by ear, including blind and low-vision people. We decoded NASA's GISTEMP v4 visualization (SVS #5207) back into real temperature anomalies for every 2°C of the planet from 1881 to 2023, and checked them against NASA's published global means (within 0.1 °C). 
   Users explore a 3D globe with the keyboard or mouse: warmer places play higher and faster, colder ones lower and slower, while a low hum follows the world average. Pressing Enter plays a whole line from pole to pole. A Listening mode built for blind users adds a narrator, game-style menus and screen-reader support; a Visual mode serves sighted users. Search, history, comparison, a guided sound tour and a "warmest spot" radar make the data easy to explore. 
   Nothing plays on its own: the user chooses the place, the year and when to listen. Earth Information Center visualizations are powerful but visual only. Degrees of Sound makes the same NASA data accessible to people who can't see it, and gives everyone a new, memorable way to sense how fast our planet is warming.
details:
HOW IT WORKS

"Degrees of Sound" turns NASA's global temperature data into music, so climate change can be explored by ear.

The user stands on a spot of a 3D globe and chooses a year between 1881 and 2023. Pressing "S" plays that spot's tune:


- Warmer than normal: higher and faster notes, played on a soft electric piano.


- Colder than normal: lower and slower notes, played on a wooden marimba.


- Normal (the 1951-1980 average): always the same note.


- A low hum underneath follows the world average temperature, so you hear the whole planet warming over the years.


- Enter plays a whole line from the North Pole to the South Pole, like running a finger across a harp.

The data comes from NASA's GISTEMP v4 temperature anomaly visualization (NASA SVS #5207). NASA publishes it as a coloured map video, not as numbers, so we built a decoder:


1. It takes one frame per year.


2. It matches every pixel's colour to NASA's colour scale.


3. It rebuilds the temperature for every 2° x 2° cell of the planet: 16,200 values per year, over 2.3 million in total.

Every year's world average is automatically checked against NASA's official figures and matches within 0.1 °C. The app uses no simulated or invented data.

There are two modes:


- Listening mode (the default) is built for blind and low-vision users. A narrator describes where you are, everything works from the keyboard, and the menus behave like game menus.


- Visual mode is for sighted users: click the globe and read the values on colour-coded gauges.

Extra built in tools:
- search for countries, regions and oceans
- 143 years of a place's history as a 10-second melody
- comparison with 1951
- a one-minute sound tour that teaches what every sound means
- a "heat radar" that points by sound to the warmest or coldest place nearby
- a CSV download of every spot's data

Nothing plays on its own: the user decides where to go, which year to hear and when the music starts.


BENEFITS

- Access for people who can't see the maps. Blind and low-vision people can explore real NASA climate data on their own, without anyone describing a picture to them.


- Real, verifiable data. Every sound comes from NASA's numbers and is checked against them.


- Works anywhere. It runs in any modern browser from a single link: no installation, no account, no server.


- Works with existing assistive technology. Users with their own screen reader (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver) can turn our narrator off and get every message through their screen reader.


- Easy to learn. One minute with the sound tour is enough to understand every sound.


- Memorable for everyone. Hearing 1900 played slow and low, then 2023 fast and high, makes warming felt rather than just read.


IMPACT

NASA's Earth Information Center visualizations are powerful but visual only. We want the same science to reach the people the maps leave out.

Short term:


- Blind and low-vision students and adults can explore climate change independently, at their own pace.


- Teachers get a new way to teach it in mixed classrooms, where sighted and non-sighted students use the same tool.

Long term:


- The decoder works for any NASA map with a colour scale, so the same approach can open up ocean temperatures, wildfires, sea ice and more.


- It could also become a museum exhibit: a globe you listen to.


TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript.


- Libraries: three.js (3D globe, WebGL), Tone.js (music, built on the Web Audio API), Google Fonts (Press Start 2P and VT323).


- Browser features: Web Speech API (narrator voice), Web Audio, WebGL, ARIA live regions (screen-reader support), localStorage (saved settings).


- Data processing: Node.js, for the decoder that converts NASA's video into data. It runs once, not in the app.


- Development: VS Code with Live Server, Git and GitHub, GitHub Pages for hosting.
- Testing: automated logic and in-browser tests (headless Microsoft Edge) and the axe-core accessibility audit (0 violations).


- Hardware: our own laptops and headphones. No special hardware is needed, for us or for users.


CREATIVITY

- We reverse-engineered a visualization back into data. Instead of looking for a ready-made dataset, we read NASA's own map video pixel by pixel. We matched colour shade rather than brightness, because land is shaded darker than ocean.


- Two clues for one meaning. Temperature changes both pitch and speed, so it's easier to hear. Instrument and note density add more information without adding confusion.


- It always sounds musical. Every note comes from a pentatonic scale, so the data can never play a "wrong" chord, even with notes from many places at once.


- Game design for accessibility. We borrowed ideas from games made for blind players: menus that read themselves out; short sound cues (a chime when crossing the equator, a thud at the edge of the map, a soft breath where there's no data); a sound radar that guides you by direction; and a narrator that waits until you stop pressing keys.


- The user is the explorer. The globe doesn't play a fixed song. Each user composes their own path through 143 years of data.


FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy over everything. We used no invented data, and we check every year automatically against NASA.


- Honesty about the numbers. NASA's map only stores differences from normal, so local values are shown as "+1.4°", not as a temperature we can't verify. Only the world average is shown in °C (about 15.1 °C in 2023), using NASA's own 14 °C baseline.


- One voice at a time. Our narrator and a user's screen reader never speak over each other.


- User control. No autoplay; every sound starts with the user's action.


- Readable design. We replaced our first pixel font because "+2.0" looked like "+8.0". Clear numbers mattered more than style. We added a plain-font option, bigger text, subtitles and support for reduced motion.


- Simplicity and reach. A single web page with no installation, so it works in schools and on any computer.


- Hackathon rules. We prepared only NASA resources before the event and wrote all code during it. We disclosed our AI use.
